patterns.title: US outage wave, Nov 12 to 17
patterns.narrative: Outages hit well-known US services within six days: Microsoft 365, the FAA ground stop, the National Weather Service, Workday, Chase, United, Marriott, Charles Schwab, Apple and the NSA's classified network, with Japan's Docomo failing on Nov 16. They are linked only by timing. Every organization that gave a cause gave its own technical one, and the Director of National Intelligence, the DHS secretary and the White House all said they see no cyberattack. Lawmakers are now pressing for explanations.
patterns.caveat: Officials say these were not attacks and not coordinated. Workday, Marriott, Schwab and United have published no cause, Google disputes a broad Gmail outage, and the FAA trigger is still undetermined, so the picture could change. A data-theft claim against JPMorgan by the n0n gang is unconfirmed and the bank says its outage was a software bug.

edges.rel: a day apart, no stated link

patterns.title: Planned changes going wrong
patterns.narrative: Five of the big outages are blamed by the organizations themselves on planned change: an earlier network capacity upgrade at Microsoft, a router replacement at the FAA, a software release at Chase, scheduled maintenance at the NSA and an internal update at Apple. The Director of National Intelligence made the same point, tying the outages to system upgrades. For defenders the lesson is change control and rollback, not threat hunting.
patterns.caveat: The causes are self-reported and the FAA trigger is still undetermined. No source says the changes share a common cause; the common factor is an inference, not a finding.

patterns.title: Knock-on effects of the Microsoft outage
patterns.narrative: Sources directly connect three later events to the Microsoft 365 outage: a high-volume phishing campaign Microsoft saw from Nov 13 posing as service-health notices about the incident, a chlorine warning email that never reached a German hotel where 15 guests were poisoned, and the pressure in Washington for explanations.
patterns.caveat: The hotel report comes from one outlet. Microsoft has not named the phishing actor or confirmed that credentials were captured.

patterns.title: AI-driven attack tooling (ARTEX, CAIRN)
patterns.narrative: The FBI, Cisco Talos, Amazon and Cloudflare each describe intrusions or scanning run with the open-source ARTEX agent platform; Cloudflare says AI pentest traffic rose about 30-fold since October. Unit 42 describes a China-nexus cluster using a fork of the Cairn framework, and Google reports the first intrusion it saw run end to end by AI agents, plus a PRC-nexus group building its own tool. Australia's ACSC warned on Nov 17 that exploitation now follows disclosure faster.
patterns.caveat: Same tools, different actors. ARTEX is open source, so shared tooling says nothing about who is behind an intrusion. The FBI and Talos both cite more than 2,250 downstream tenants but describe the case differently; that they are one case is our inference.

patterns.title: Fireworks AI breach reaching its customers
patterns.narrative: Fireworks AI confirmed two intrusions on Nov 17, the second exposing account and billing data for every account created before Oct 30. Three customers are tied to it by their own or reported statements: Cursor says a key it issued to Fireworks was exposed and led to trojanized Claude Code extension builds; Notion says some AI chat transcripts were accessed; and SecurityWeek reports an Uber spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that its breach of about 150,000 people involved Fireworks AI.
patterns.caveat: Sources do not always say which of the two Fireworks incidents reached each customer. Uber's own notices did not name the provider; the link rests on a spokesperson statement reported second-hand.

patterns.title: Developer and AI-agent toolchains as the target
patterns.narrative: Several separate incidents aim at the tools developers and AI agents run with: trojanized Claude Code extension builds in Cursor's marketplace cache, a credential stealer in Microsoft's Agent Framework package on PyPI, a North Korean cluster planting a backdoor through Claude Code settings files, 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts pushing a CI secrets stealer, and scanning for LiteLLM flaws, one of which CISA has now listed as exploited. Microsoft also showed in a lab how one phished device-code approval could steer a coding agent. The prize in each is the keys and tokens these tools hold.
patterns.caveat: These are different actors and methods; no source connects them. The Microsoft device-code work is a proof of concept, not an attack seen in the wild, and the LiteLLM flaw SANS saw probed is not the one CISA listed.

patterns.title: One vendor, many victims
patterns.narrative: Many of the week's confirmed breaches came through a supplier rather than the front door: Optimizely's script reached 178 organizations, Belfast supplier Wellington IT is reported to have exposed about 40 Irish credit unions, Visa says its incident was at an Asia Pacific provider, and Fireworks AI reached Cursor, Notion and Uber. TSMC, Iris Ohyama, Infoblox, Maileva, Osaka and PLAID's KARTE also involve a provider, and remote-management tools N-able and ScreenConnect show the same logic.
patterns.caveat: These are separate vendors and separate attackers; the shared element is the route, not the actor. Several victims have not named their provider, so two of them sharing one cannot be ruled in or out.

patterns.title: From disclosure to exploitation
patterns.narrative: Fixes are turning into attacks quickly. The Apache Axis flaw Rapid7 saw used against Confluence on Nov 13 was added to CISA's exploited list on Nov 18, and Rapid7 reports N-able N-central exploited alongside it. Check Point's Gaia flaw used to wipe gateways went on the list a day after disclosure. CISA told everyone to patch Java4Shell at once, with the fix in Oracle's November update. Apache Roller and Apache's mod_http2 are reported exploited, and public exploit code exists for NGINX over HTTP/2, Ivanti Endpoint Manager and Drupal core.
patterns.caveat: Each link is to a specific flaw and is stated by an agency or vendor. Rapid7 says the N-able and Confluence exploitation was reported together, not that one actor did both. No exploitation is reported yet for NGINX, Drupal or F5 BIG-IP.

edges.rel: Gaia flaw in chain listed as exploited

patterns.title: Refrigeration controllers under attack
patterns.narrative: Midnight Blue says attack waves on internet-exposed refrigeration controllers started in France on Oct 11, and this week disclosed six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in Danfoss controllers. VulnCheck disclosed 14 flaws in end-of-life Copeland XWEB EVO supervisors and saw two targeted within a day. France says it will seek EU sanctions on an IRGC cyber unit over the French attacks, and Italy's prime minister briefed the opposition on hybrid threats after supermarket and school incidents.
patterns.caveat: The attribution to an IRGC unit is the French government's; Iran routinely denies such operations and Midnight Blue says attribution remains open. No source ties the Copeland probing to the French campaign. The October attacks themselves are outside the map's window.

edges.rel: controllers hit in French attack waves

patterns.title: State-linked espionage and North Korean theft
patterns.narrative: Google and Mandiant show Russia's COLD RELIC using data stolen from one US organisation to phish a second. Unit 42 and Kaspersky describe espionage against Asian and other governments using HTTP/3 tools and backdoors hidden in GitHub and SharePoint traffic. On North Korea, the Justice Department disrupted the FaceStealer fake-meeting scheme the FBI detailed the same day, Google describes a cluster backdooring crypto developers, and Talos tracks a crypto-stealing group it ties to North Korea with low confidence.
patterns.caveat: Only DOJ and FBI on FaceStealer describe the same operation. The North Korean reports name different clusters, and Talos's attribution is low confidence. The other reports are separate research grouped by type, some describing older activity.

patterns.title: Extortion claims and the law-enforcement response
patterns.narrative: Leak sites posted claims in batches: on Nov 17 Vortex listed six US companies within minutes and Inception listed AMD, Cigna, Paychex and PepsiCo; n0n listed Visa, JPMorgan, Verastem and Exelixis; The Gentlemen listed Nvidia, days after CERT-In's advisory on that group. Kaspersky described AuditTeam, which dresses ransom up as an audit fee. In the same week Operation Endgame took down Gootloader, which the FBI then detailed, Europol announced 354 dark-web arrests, and the US won an extradition and a sentencing.
patterns.caveat: Most listings are unverified attacker claims; Visa says its incident was at a provider and no card numbers were affected. Batch timing shows when listings appeared, not when or how intrusions happened. The arrests are not tied to these groups.

patterns.title: Healthcare breach notices cluster
patterns.narrative: US healthcare organizations kept disclosing breaches: Access Dental Management (341,049 people), Minnesota Epilepsy Group's second of the year, Dorsata through a Metabase zero-day, Hood River Dental with two, LifeTouch Health, Geisinger, MPOWERHealth and Lansing Urgent Care. Outside the US a German hospital closed its emergency room after a cyberattack. Health data remains the most frequently notified category on the map.
patterns.caveat: Many underlying intrusions date from 2025 to September 2026, so the cluster reflects when notices went out, not a new wave. The cases have different causes and no source connects them.

analysis.summary: The US outage wave remains a cluster in time only: each organization gives its own non-cyber cause, and senior officials say there was no attack. Confirmed attacks follow two routes: a compromised supplier reaching many customers (Fireworks AI to Cursor, Notion and Uber; Optimizely; Wellington IT and Irish credit unions) and fast exploitation of new flaws, with the Confluence Apache Axis flaw now on CISA's exploited list and Java4Shell under an immediate-patch alert. Developer and AI-agent tools are a growing target, from a poisoned PyPI package to backdoored Claude Code settings. France's push to sanction Iran over refrigeration attacks is the week's clearest government attribution; leak-site batches and healthcare notices are patterns of timing only.

direct: Any service that decodes untrusted Base64 on an affected x86-64 HotSpot Java runtime could be crashed or taken over without a login.
downstream: Java is bundled inside third-party applications, appliances and container images, so exposure extends to products you did not build.
Patching depends on each vendor shipping an updated runtime, so some systems will stay exposed after your own servers are fixed.
watch_for: Unexpected JVM crashes and restarts
Vendor advisories naming a bundled Java runtime
Signs of exploitation reported by CISA or vendors

direct: Self-hosted Confluence Data Center with the Remote API enabled can be taken over without a login; CISA lists the Axis flaw as exploited.
downstream: In the case Rapid7 saw, the intruder took database credentials, queried a cloud data warehouse and signed in to Microsoft 365 as a service account.
Apache Axis 1.x is end-of-life and may sit inside other Java products that will not get a fix.
watch_for: Unusual Remote API requests to Confluence
Service accounts signing in from new places
Other products bundling Apache Axis 1.x

direct: Internet-facing N-central servers were exploited through zero-days published without coordinated disclosure; crypto miners were deployed.
downstream: An RMM server reaches every managed client, so a compromise can spread to many customer networks at once.
Removal of the Legacy API may break older integrations that still depend on it.
watch_for: N-central servers not on Hotfix 3
New agents or scripts pushed from RMM
Mining processes on managed endpoints

direct: Account and billing data for every Fireworks AI account created before Oct 30 was exposed; some customers' secrets, model files and datasets were reached earlier.
downstream: Cursor, Notion and Uber are reported as affected customers; keys held by the provider led to a trojanized extension at Cursor.
Credentials pasted into AI prompts or held by inference providers can open systems far from the provider itself.
watch_for: Notices from AI and inference providers you use
Use of API keys issued to providers
Secrets in AI chat logs and traces

direct: Agent Framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI ran a credential stealer at Python start-up, aimed at cloud, GitHub and AI tokens.
downstream: Any CI job or developer machine that installed those versions may have leaked tokens that unlock cloud accounts and repositories.
Unpinned dependencies pull a bad release automatically, so exposure can exist without anyone choosing to upgrade.
watch_for: Installs of versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2
Token use from unfamiliar hosts after Nov 17
Unpinned AI packages in build files

direct: Malicious JavaScript was injected into some Optimizely Web Experimentation customer projects, reaching 178 organisations by one researcher's count.
downstream: Coverage says the code skimmed payment cards and swapped crypto addresses on customers' sites, so their visitors were the victims.
Sites that load third-party scripts without integrity checks or a strict Content-Security-Policy inherit the supplier's compromise.
watch_for: Unexpected scripts on checkout pages
CSP violation reports
Notices from script and tag vendors

direct: Saved payee records at about 40 Irish credit unions were exposed through a reported attack on supplier Wellington IT.
downstream: Payee data can be used to make fraud and impersonation messages to members more convincing.
Ireland's finance minister called the delay unacceptable, so expect regulatory scrutiny of supplier notification.
watch_for: Payment-redirection and impersonation lures to members
Statements from the supplier or the Central Bank
Automated API abuse with valid logins

direct: NGINX Open Source and Plus with HTTP/2 can be taken over without a login; a public proof of concept exists for one flaw.
downstream: NGINX sits in front of many sites and is embedded in load balancers, ingress controllers and appliances that update on vendors' schedules.
A public proof of concept usually shortens the time before scanning and attacks begin.
watch_for: Ingress and appliance vendors shipping fixed NGINX
Worker crashes on HTTP/2 traffic
Reports of in-the-wild exploitation

direct: Six unpatched pre-authentication flaws let attackers take over Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers; hundreds are reachable online.
downstream: Food retail, cold storage and pharmacies risk spoiled stock and safety incidents; French attacks on such controllers were linked to fires.
France is seeking EU sanctions over the campaign, which could prompt further attacks or warnings.
watch_for: Refrigeration controllers reachable from the internet
Unexpected setpoint or alarm changes
CVE numbers and fixes from Danfoss

direct: Equinor's IT systems are under an ongoing attack; it says production is unaffected and email was reported down.
downstream: Restoration time is unknown, so partners and suppliers may see delays or unusual messages from Equinor.
Attackers often use a known incident to send fake invoices or updates in the victim's name.
watch_for: Messages claiming to come from Equinor
Norwegian authority advisories
Any named attacker or leak claim
